claim: The C. elegans egg-laying circuit consists of four type 1 vulval muscle cells (vm1) and four type 2 vulval muscle cells (vm2).
source: The C. elegans egg-laying circuit consists four type 1 vulval muscle cells (vm1) and four type 2 vulval muscle cells (vm2), which form two X-shaped structures near the vulval opening (Figure 1A).
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text with reference to Figure 1A showing the circuit organization.

claim: vm1 and vm2 form two X-shaped structures near the vulval opening.
source: The C. elegans egg-laying circuit consists four type 1 vulval muscle cells (vm1) and four type 2 vulval muscle cells (vm2), which form two X-shaped structures near the vulval opening (Figure 1A).
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text with reference to Figure 1A.

claim: vm1 and vm2 are from a common lineage.
source: While vm1 and vm2 are from a common lineage, are physically adjacent and share many molecular components, the egg-laying motoneurons HSN and VC4/5 form serotoninergic and cholinergic chemical synapses exclusively on vm2 (White et al., 1986; Waggoner et al., 1998; Duerr et al., 2001; Kim et al., 2001).
evidence: Stated in the manuscript text with citation to White et al., 1986.

claim: vm1 and vm2 are physically adjacent.
source: While vm1 and vm2 are from a common lineage, are physically adjacent and share many molecular components, the egg-laying motoneurons HSN and VC4/5 form serotoninergic and cholinergic chemical synapses exclusively on vm2 (White et al., 1986; Waggoner et al., 1998; Duerr et al., 2001; Kim et al., 2001).
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text.

claim: vm1 and vm2 share many molecular components.
source: While vm1 and vm2 are from a common lineage, are physically adjacent and share many molecular components, the egg-laying motoneurons HSN and VC4/5 form serotoninergic and cholinergic chemical synapses exclusively on vm2 (White et al., 1986; Waggoner et al., 1998; Duerr et al., 2001; Kim et al., 2001).
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text.

claim: HSN and VC4/5 form serotoninergic and cholinergic chemical synapses exclusively on vm2.
source: While vm1 and vm2 are from a common lineage, are physically adjacent and share many molecular components, the egg-laying motoneurons HSN and VC4/5 form serotoninergic and cholinergic chemical synapses exclusively on vm2 (White et al., 1986; Waggoner et al., 1998; Duerr et al., 2001; Kim et al., 2001).
evidence: Stated in the manuscript text with citations to multiple prior studies.

claim: vm1 is mainly controlled by vm2 via gap junctions.
source: vm1 is mainly controlled by vm2 via gap junctions (White et al., 1986).
evidence: Stated in the manuscript text with citation to White et al., 1986.

claim: vm2 receives some additional synapses with the ventral nerve cord.
source: Besides forming major synaptic connection on HSN and VC4/5, vm2 also receive some additional synapses with the ventral nerve cord (Personal communication with Michael Koelle, November 2012).
evidence: Stated in the manuscript text with citation to personal communication.

claim: HSN presynaptic specializations are closely juxtaposed against the dendritic spine-like membrane protrusions (muscle arms) from the vm2 cell bodies.
source: Consistent with EM reconstruction, we found that the HSN presynaptic specializations were closely juxtaposed against the dendritic spine-like membrane protrusions (muscle arms) from the vm2 cell bodies when viewed from both the lateral and ventral sides (Figure 1B).
evidence: Stated in the manuscript text with reference to Figure 1B showing the juxtaposition.

claim: The muscle arms always extend from stereotyped subcellular locations, medially towards the center of the vulva.
source: The muscle arms always extend from stereotyped subcellular locations, medially towards the center of the vulva.
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text.

claim: The muscle arms from the anterior and posterior vm2 cells often contact each other and form a 'bridge-like' structure.
source: The muscle arms from the anterior and posterior vm2 cells often contact each other and form a 'bridge-like' structure that is best visualized from the ventral view (Figure 1B,C, top row).
evidence: Stated in the manuscript text with reference to Figure 1B,C showing the bridge-like structure.

claim: VC4/5 presynaptic specializations are closely apposed to vm2 muscle arms.
source: Similar apposition was also observed between VC4/5 presynaptic specializations and the vm2 muscle arms (Figure 1C).
evidence: Stated in the manuscript text with reference to Figure 1C.

claim: UNC-103E is dramatically enriched on vm2 muscle arms.
source: While high level of UNC-103E::GFP expression labels both the muscle arms and the vm cell bodies (Figure 1C), low level of transgenic expression of UNC-103E::GFP with an integrated single-copy transgene showed that UNC-103E was dramatically enriched on vm2 muscle arms (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, middle), indicating that the muscle arms represent functional postsynaptic specializations (Collins and Koelle, 2012).
evidence: Stated in the manuscript text with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1 showing enrichment.

claim: The muscle arms represent functional postsynaptic specializations.
source: While high level of UNC-103E::GFP expression labels both the muscle arms and the vm cell bodies (Figure 1C), low level of transgenic expression of UNC-103E::GFP with an integrated single-copy transgene showed that UNC-103E was dramatically enriched on vm2 muscle arms (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, middle), indicating that the muscle arms represent functional postsynaptic specializations (Collins and Koelle, 2012).
evidence: Stated in the manuscript text with citation to Collins and Koelle, 2012.

claim: HSN axon guidance and presynaptic formation preceded both axon growth of VC neurons and vulval muscle differentiation.
source: Developmental studies showed that HSN axon guidance and presynaptic formation preceded both axon growth of VC neurons and vulval muscle differentiation (data not shown).
evidence: Stated in the manuscript text based on developmental studies.

claim: In egl-1(n986) mutants, the morphology and position of vm2 muscle arms are indistinguishable from wild type.
source: Surprisingly, in all of the examined animals, the morphology and position of vm2 muscle arms were indistinguishable from the wild type counterparts (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Stated in the manuscript text with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 2A showing the phenotype.

claim: In egl-1(n986) mutants, HSN neurons undergo programmed cell death in embryonic stage.
source: We therefore asked whether the HSN neurons are required for vm2 specification and muscle arm development by examining the vm2 morphology in the egl-1(n986) mutant, in which the HSN neurons undergo programmed cell death in embryonic stage (Conradt and Horvitz, 1998).
evidence: Stated in the manuscript text with citation to Conradt and Horvitz, 1998.

claim: In egl-1(n986);lin-39(n709) double mutants lacking both HSN and VC neurons, vm2 muscle arms still exist.
source: First, in a portion of the egl-1(n986);lin-39(n709) double mutant animals which lacked both HSN and VC neurons (Clark et al., 1993), the vm2 muscle arms still existed (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Stated in the manuscript text with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 2B and citation to Clark et al., 1993.

claim: In unc-104(e1265) mutants, synaptic vesicles are absent from the presynaptic regions in both HSN and VC neurons.
source: Second, in unc-104(e1265) mutant animals, in which the synaptic vesicles were absent from the presynaptic regions in both HSN and VC neurons (Shen and Bargmann, 2003), vm2 muscle arm development was not affected (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Stated in the manuscript text with citation to Shen and Bargmann, 2003.

claim: In unc-104(e1265) mutants, vm2 muscle arm development is not affected.
source: Second, in unc-104(e1265) mutant animals, in which the synaptic vesicles were absent from the presynaptic regions in both HSN and VC neurons (Shen and Bargmann, 2003), vm2 muscle arm development was not affected (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Stated in the manuscript text with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Presynaptic components are dispensable for vm2 postsynaptic development.
source: These results indicate that presynaptic components are dispensable for vm2 postsynaptic development.
evidence: Conclusion stated in the manuscript text based on the experimental results.

claim: In lin-3(e1417) mutants, vulval epithelial cell fate is abnormal.
source: We examined the vm2 muscle arm morphology in lin-3(e1417) mutant animals, in which vulval epithelial cell fate is abnormal (Hill and Sternberg, 1992), and observed severe defects on both vulval muscle morphology and muscle arm development (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Stated in the manuscript text with citation to Hill and Sternberg, 1992.

claim: In lin-3(e1417) mutants, severe defects on both vulval muscle morphology and muscle arm development are observed.
source: We examined the vm2 muscle arm morphology in lin-3(e1417) mutant animals, in which vulval epithelial cell fate is abnormal (Hill and Sternberg, 1992), and observed severe defects on both vulval muscle morphology and muscle arm development (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Stated in the manuscript text with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Vulval epithelial cells are required for normal vulval muscle differentiation and morphogenesis.
source: This result suggests that the vulval epithelial cells are required for normal vulval muscle differentiation and morphogenesis, and therefore might be also important for vm2 postsynaptic muscle arm development.
evidence: Conclusion stated in the manuscript text based on the lin-3(e1417) mutant phenotype.

claim: Six individual mutants representing three complementation groups were isolated in which the vm2 muscle arms were largely absent.
source: In total, six individual mutants representing three complementation groups were isolated in which the vm2 muscle arms were largely absent (Figure 1D,E and Table 1).
evidence: Stated in the manuscript text with reference to Figure 1D,E and Table 1.

claim: The isolated mutations affected genes in LIN-12/Notch signaling pathway including lin-12/Notch, apx-1/DSL and sel-12/presinilin.
source: Mapping and molecular identification of these mutations showed that they affected genes in LIN-12/Notch signaling pathway including lin-12/Notch, apx-1/DSL and sel-12/presinilin (Table 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Stated in the manuscript text with reference to Table 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: In lin-12(wy750) mutants, the SER-1B::GFP labeled vm2 muscle arm structures are completely absent.
source: In lin-12(wy750) mutant animals, while the muscle morphology of both vm1 and vm2 were largely normal, the SER-1B::GFP labeled vm2 muscle arm structures were completely absent (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: Stated in the manuscript text with reference to Figure 1D,E.

claim: In lin-12(wy750) mutants, the muscle morphology of both vm1 and vm2 are largely normal.
source: In lin-12(wy750) mutant animals, while the muscle morphology of both vm1 and vm2 were largely normal, the SER-1B::GFP labeled vm2 muscle arm structures were completely absent (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: Stated in the manuscript text with reference to Figure 1D,E.

claim: In lin-12(wy750) mutants, the single-copy insertion of the transgene UNC-103E::GFP potassium channel is completely absent in the muscle arm areas.
source: Furthermore, the single-copy insertion of the transgene UNC-103E::GFP potassium channel which specifically labels the vm2 muscle arms, as well as the artificial membrane marker mCD8::mCherry that delineates the entire outline of vulval muscles, was also completely absent in the muscle arm areas, suggestive of a complete loss of the muscle arm structure (Figure 1F).
evidence: Stated in the manuscript text with reference to Figure 1F.

claim: In lin-12(wy750) mutants, the artificial membrane marker mCD8::mCherry is completely absent in the muscle arm areas.
source: Furthermore, the single-copy insertion of the transgene UNC-103E::GFP potassium channel which specifically labels the vm2 muscle arms, as well as the artificial membrane marker mCD8::mCherry that delineates the entire outline of vulval muscles, was also completely absent in the muscle arm areas, suggestive of a complete loss of the muscle arm structure (Figure 1F).
evidence: Stated in the manuscript text with reference to Figure 1F.

claim: Both HSN and VC presynaptic markers appear normal in the lin-12(wy750) mutant.
source: Both HSN and VC presynaptic markers appeared normal in the lin-12(wy750) mutant, indicating that the mutation specifically affected postsynaptic differentiation and development (Figure 1—figure supplement 4B,D).
evidence: Stated in the manuscript text with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 4B,D.

claim: The lin-12(wy750) mutation specifically affects postsynaptic differentiation and development.
source: Both HSN and VC presynaptic markers appeared normal in the lin-12(wy750) mutant, indicating that the mutation specifically affected postsynaptic differentiation and development (Figure 1—figure supplement 4B,D).
evidence: Conclusion stated in the manuscript text based on the observation that presynaptic markers are normal.

claim: No vulval morphogenesis defect was found in lin-12(wy750) mutants by differential interference contrast (DIC) microscopy or the localization pattern of the ajm-1::gfp apical junction marker.
source: Surprisingly, we found no vulval morphogenesis defect in lin-12(wy750) mutants either by differential interference contrast (DIC) microscopy or the localization pattern of the ajm-1::gfp apical junction marker at several development stages (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A and data not shown) (Koppen et al., 2001).
evidence: Stated in the manuscript text with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 4A and citation to Koppen et al., 2001.

claim: apx-1(wy750) and sel-12(wy760) mutants are similar to the lin-12(wy750) mutant in their specific defective vm2 muscle arm development and normal vulval muscle development.
source: Two other mutants isolated from the same screen, apx-1(wy750) and sel-12(wy760), were very similar to the lin-12(wy750) mutant in their specific defective vm2 muscle arm development and normal vulval muscle development (Figure 1D and data not shown).
evidence: Stated in the manuscript text with reference to Figure 1D.

claim: Vulval muscles, together with the uterine muscles, are produced through three rounds of cell divisions from a single sex myoblast cell.
source: Vulval muscles, together with the uterine muscles, are produced through three rounds of cell divisions from a single sex myoblast cell, which is derived from the postembryonic mesodermal lineage (M lineage).
evidence: Stated in the manuscript text.

claim: The sex myoblast cell is derived from the postembryonic mesodermal lineage (M lineage).
source: Vulval muscles, together with the uterine muscles, are produced through three rounds of cell divisions from a single sex myoblast cell, which is derived from the postembryonic mesodermal lineage (M lineage).
evidence: Stated in the manuscript text.

claim: In lin-12(wy750) mutants, all three markers (hlh-8::gfp, egl-15::gfp, and rgs-2::gfp) exhibit wild type pattern.
source: In lin-12(wy750) mutants, all three markers exhibits wild type pattern, suggesting that many molecular signatures of the M lineage are intact in the lin-12(wy750) mutants, while the development of the postsynaptic specializations completely fails (Figure 1—figure supplement 4C,E,F).
evidence: Stated in the manuscript text with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 4C,E,F.

claim: Many molecular signatures of the M lineage are intact in the lin-12(wy750) mutants.
source: In lin-12(wy750) mutants, all three markers exhibits wild type pattern, suggesting that many molecular signatures of the M lineage are intact in the lin-12(wy750) mutants, while the development of the postsynaptic specializations completely fails (Figure 1—figure supplement 4C,E,F).
evidence: Conclusion stated in the manuscript text based on the marker expression patterns.

claim: No significant difference was found on the intersection angle between the vulval muscle and the vulval slit in lin-12(wy750) mutants compared to wild type.
source: No significant difference was found on the intersection angle between the vulval muscle and the vulval slit, as well as the relative size of vm2 to vm1 (Svm2/Svm1) (Figure 1—figure supplement 6).
evidence: Stated in the manuscript text with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 6.

claim: No significant difference was found on the relative size of vm2 to vm1 (Svm2/Svm1) in lin-12(wy750) mutants compared to wild type.
source: No significant difference was found on the intersection angle between the vulval muscle and the vulval slit, as well as the relative size of vm2 to vm1 (Svm2/Svm1) (Figure 1—figure supplement 6).
evidence: Stated in the manuscript text with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 6.

claim: The muscle arm defective mutants laid notably fewer eggs compared to the wild-type animals.
source: First, the muscle arm defective mutants laid notably fewer eggs compared to the wild-type animals (Figure 2A).
evidence: Stated in the manuscript text with reference to Figure 2A.

claim: The muscle arm defective mutants laid more late-stage eggs and fewer early-stage eggs compared with wild-type animals.
source: Indeed, we found that these mutants laid more late-stage eggs and fewer early-stage eggs compared with wild-type animals (Figure 2B), indicative of defects in the egg-laying circuit.
evidence: Stated in the manuscript text with reference to Figure 2B.

claim: In wild-type animals, simultaneous Ca2+ transients in the anterior and posterior vulval muscles drive synchronous muscle contraction and release of eggs.
source: In wild-type animals, simultaneous Ca2+ transients in the anterior and posterior vulval muscles, which we call 'double' transients, drive synchronous muscle contraction and release of eggs (Collins and Koelle, 2012) (Figure 2C).
evidence: Stated in the manuscript text with reference to Figure 2C and citation to Collins and Koelle, 2012.

claim: lin-12(wy750) and apx-1(wy755) vm2 muscle arm mutants are still able to execute single anterior and posterior vulval muscle Ca2+ transients.
source: Despite their lack of postsynaptic muscle arms, we found that lin-12(wy750) and apx-1(wy755) vm2 muscle arm mutants were still able to execute single anterior and posterior vulval muscle Ca2+ transients, which was presumably due to the intact minor synaptic inputs from the ventral nerve cord alongside the vulval muscles (Collins and Koelle, 2012).
evidence: Stated in the manuscript text with citation to Collins and Koelle, 2012.

claim: In lin-12(wy750) and apx-1(wy755) mutants, double Ca2+ transients are often asynchronous, with significant delays between anterior and posterior vulval muscle transients.
source: However, double Ca2+ transients were often asynchronous, with significant delays between anterior and posterior vulval muscle transients that resulted in uncoordinated vulval muscle contractions that were not able to release eggs (Figure 2D and Video 2).
evidence: Stated in the manuscript text with reference to Figure 2D and Video 2.

claim: lin-12(wy750) and apx-1(wy755) mutants had a twofold increase in the frequency of Ca2+ transient peaks.
source: As a result, lin-12(wy750) and apx-1(wy755) mutants had a twofold increase in the frequency of Ca2+ transient peaks (Figure 2H).
evidence: Stated in the manuscript text with reference to Figure 2H.

claim: lin-12(wy750) and apx-1(wy755) mutants had significantly fewer synchronous double transients compared to the wild type.
source: We also found that lin-12(wy750) and apx-1(wy755) mutants had significantly fewer synchronous double transients compared to the wild type (Figure 2I).
evidence: Stated in the manuscript text with reference to Figure 2I.

claim: In wild-type animals, the average anterior/posterior delay in double Ca2+ transients is only ∼100 ms.
source: In wild-type animals, the average anterior/posterior delay was only ∼100 ms (Figure 2J), as nearly all double transients were not resolved into separate anterior/posterior peaks at the temporal and spatial resolution of our ΔR/R traces (Figure 2E).
evidence: Stated in the manuscript text with reference to Figure 2J.

claim: In both lin-12(wy750) and apx-1(wy755) mutants, the average anterior/posterior delay in double Ca2+ transients increased to ∼800 ms.
source: In both lin-12(wy750) and apx-1(wy755) mutants, the average anterior/posterior delay in double Ca2+ transients increased to ∼800 ms (Figure 2J) and anterior/posterior transients were easily resolved (Figure 2F,G).
evidence: Stated in the manuscript text with reference to Figure 2J.

claim: The vm2 muscle arms are not necessary for excitation of the vulval muscles.
source: Together, these results show that the vm2 muscle arms lacking in lin-12(wy750) and apx-1(wy755) mutants are not necessary for excitation of the vulval muscles, but suggest they are required for the synchronous excitation of anterior and posterior vulval muscles needed to successfully execute egg-laying behavior.
evidence: Conclusion stated in the manuscript text based on the Ca2+ imaging results.

claim: The vm2 muscle arms are required for the synchronous excitation of anterior and posterior vulval muscles needed to successfully execute egg-laying behavior.
source: Together, these results show that the vm2 muscle arms lacking in lin-12(wy750) and apx-1(wy755) mutants are not necessary for excitation of the vulval muscles, but suggest they are required for the synchronous excitation of anterior and posterior vulval muscles needed to successfully execute egg-laying behavior.
evidence: Conclusion stated in the manuscript text based on the Ca2+ imaging results.

claim: lin-12(wy750) contains a single missense mutation (G473R) in one of the conserved extracellular EGF domains of the LIN-12 protein.
source: Sequence analyses revealed that lin-12(wy750) contained a single missense mutation (G473R) in one of the conserved extracellular EGF domains of the LIN-12 protein (Table 1).
evidence: Stated in the manuscript text with reference to Table 1.

claim: lin-12(wy750) is a loss-of-function allele.
source: Two additional results indicated that lin-12(wy750) was a loss-of-function allele. First, trans-heterozygotes between lin-12(wy750) and a canonical loss-of-function allele lin-12(n676n930) presented similar muscle arm defects (data not shown). Second, a lin-12 genomic fragment including 5 kb of upstream regulatory sequence and the entire coding region of lin-12 strongly rescued the muscle arm phenotype of lin-12(wy750) mutants (Figure 4A).
evidence: Conclusion stated in the manuscript text based on trans-heterozygote analysis and rescue experiments.

claim: A lin-12 genomic fragment including 5 kb of upstream regulatory sequence and the entire coding region of lin-12 strongly rescued the muscle arm phenotype of lin-12(wy750) mutants.
source: Second, a lin-12 genomic fragment including 5 kb of upstream regulatory sequence and the entire coding region of lin-12 strongly rescued the muscle arm phenotype of lin-12(wy750) mutants (Figure 4A).
evidence: Stated in the manuscript text with reference to Figure 4A.

claim: Three apx-1 mutant alleles independently identified from the screen contain missense mutations in the extracellular domain.
source: Three apx-1 mutant alleles independently identified from the screen also contain missense mutations in the extracellular domain.
evidence: Stated in the manuscript text.

claim: One early-stop mutation in the sel-12 coding region leads to additional pleiotropic effects on both vulval muscle patterning and vulval morphogenesis.
source: One early-stop mutation in the sel-12 coding region leads to additional pleiotropic effects on both vulval muscle patterning and vulval morphogenesis, while the other missense mutation of sel-12 causes specific muscle arm defect (Table 1).
evidence: Stated in the manuscript text with reference to Table 1.

claim: The other missense mutation of sel-12 causes specific muscle arm defect.
source: One early-stop mutation in the sel-12 coding region leads to additional pleiotropic effects on both vulval muscle patterning and vulval morphogenesis, while the other missense mutation of sel-12 causes specific muscle arm defect (Table 1).
evidence: Stated in the manuscript text with reference to Table 1.

claim: Partial loss of LIN-12/Notch signaling activity spares vulval morphogenesis but specifically impairs vm2 specification and muscle arm development.
source: Together, these data suggest that partial loss of LIN-12/Notch signaling activity spares vulval morphogenesis but specifically impairs vm2 specification and muscle arm development, and that muscle arm development might require a higher level of LIN-12/Notch signaling activity compared with earlier developmental events (see 'Discussion').
evidence: Conclusion stated in the manuscript text based on the mutant phenotypes.

claim: Muscle arm development might require a higher level of LIN-12/Notch signaling activity compared with earlier developmental events.
source: Together, these data suggest that partial loss of LIN-12/Notch signaling activity spares vulval morphogenesis but specifically impairs vm2 specification and muscle arm development, and that muscle arm development might require a higher level of LIN-12/Notch signaling activity compared with earlier developmental events (see 'Discussion').
evidence: Hypothesis stated in the manuscript text based on the mutant phenotypes.

claim: lin-12(n676n930) mutant animals grown at the permissive temperature (15°C) have no egg-laying defect and show intact vulval muscle morphology and vm2 muscle arms.
source: Consistent with previous behavioral studies, lin-12(n676n930) mutant animals grown at the permissive temperature had no egg-laying defect and showed intact vulval muscle morphology and vm2 muscle arms, whereas animals grown at the restrictive temperature retained significantly more unlaid eggs inside their bodies and displayed vulval morphogenesis and vulval muscle arm defects.
evidence: Stated in the manuscript text.

claim: lin-12(n676n930) mutant animals grown at the restrictive temperature (25°C) retain significantly more unlaid eggs inside their bodies and display vulval morphogenesis and vulval muscle arm defects.
source: Consistent with previous behavioral studies, lin-12(n676n930) mutant animals grown at the permissive temperature had no egg-laying defect and showed intact vulval muscle morphology and vm2 muscle arms, whereas animals grown at the restrictive temperature retained significantly more unlaid eggs inside their bodies and displayed vulval morphogenesis and vulval muscle arm defects.
evidence: Stated in the manuscript text.

claim: Most of the animals shifted from 15°C to 25°C prior to mid-L4 stage showed muscle arm defects similar to those of lin-12(wy750).
source: Most of the animals shifted from 15°C to 25°C prior to mid-L4 stage showed muscle arm defects similar to those of lin-12(wy750), whereas the wild-type muscle arm phenotype was observed in most of lin-12(n676n930) animals that were shifted after mid-L4 stage (Figure 3A).
evidence: Stated in the manuscript text with reference to Figure 3A.

claim: The wild-type muscle arm phenotype was observed in most of lin-12(n676n930) animals that were shifted from 15°C to 25°C after mid-L4 stage.
source: Most of the animals shifted from 15°C to 25°C prior to mid-L4 stage showed muscle arm defects similar to those of lin-12(wy750), whereas the wild-type muscle arm phenotype was observed in most of lin-12(n676n930) animals that were shifted after mid-L4 stage (Figure 3A).
evidence: Stated in the manuscript text with reference to Figure 3A.

claim: More than 80% of the animals still showed defective muscle arms when shifted from 25°C to 15°C at mid-L4.
source: More than 80% of the animals still showed defective muscle arms when shifted from 25°C to 15°C at mid-L4 (Figure 3B).
evidence: Stated in the manuscript text with reference to Figure 3B.

claim: The upshift and downshift experiments together suggest a novel function of lin-12 at the L4 stage in regulating the postsynaptic muscle arm development and synaptic target choice.
source: The upshift and downshift experiments together suggest a novel function of lin-12 at the L4 stage in regulating the postsynaptic muscle arm development and synaptic target choice.
evidence: Conclusion stated in the manuscript text based on the temperature shift experiments.

claim: This lin-12 function is independent of other known roles of lin-12, all of which occur prior to early-L4 stage.
source: This lin-12 function is independent of other known roles of lin-12, all of which occur prior to early-L4 stage.
evidence: Conclusion stated in the manuscript text based on the temperature shift experiments.

claim: The recombineered fosmid lin-12::SL2::mCherry fully rescued the lin-12 muscle arm phenotype.
source: A type II short trans-splicing leader sequence followed by mCherry (SL2::mCherry) was inserted into a fosmid containing the lin-12 genomic sequence at the 3′ end of the lin-12 coding region (lin-12::SL2::mCherry). This recombineered fosmid fully rescued the lin-12 muscle arm phenotype (Figure 4A and data not shown), suggesting that this construct should contain all upstream, downstream and intronic regulatory elements crucial for proper expression and function of lin-12.
evidence: Stated in the manuscript text with reference to Figure 4A.

claim: Transgenic animals carrying the lin-12::SL2::mCherry construct showed mCherry expression in both the vm2 muscle cells and the vulval epithelial cells.
source: Transgenic animals carrying this construct showed mCherry expression in a number of cell types including both the vm2 muscle cells (outlined by dashed lines in Figure 4A,B) and the vulval epithelial cells (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: Stated in the manuscript text with reference to Figure 4A,B.

claim: No detectable lin-12 expression was observed in vm1 muscle cells.
source: Strikingly, no detectable lin-12 expression was observed in vm1 muscle cells.
evidence: Stated in the manuscript text.

claim: Forty-five of 48 animals with lin-12 expressed in the vm2 cells (vm2+) showed a rescued, wild-type muscle arms.
source: Forty-five of 48 animals with lin-12 expressed in the vm2 cells (vm2+) showed a rescued, wild-type muscle arms (Figure 4A,C), whereas the muscle arm defect was never rescued in any of the examined animals (>50) lacking lin-12 expression in the vm2 cell (vm2-) (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: Stated in the manuscript text with reference to Figure 4A,C.

claim: The muscle arm defect was never rescued in any of the examined animals (>50) lacking lin-12 expression in the vm2 cell (vm2-).
source: Forty-five of 48 animals with lin-12 expressed in the vm2 cells (vm2+) showed a rescued, wild-type muscle arms (Figure 4A,C), whereas the muscle arm defect was never rescued in any of the examined animals (>50) lacking lin-12 expression in the vm2 cell (vm2-) (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: Stated in the manuscript text with reference to Figure 4B,C.

claim: lin-12 expression in vulval epithelial cells was not correlated with the rescue of the muscle arm defects.
source: On the contrary, lin-12 expression in vulval epithelial cells was not correlated with the rescue of the muscle arm defects (data not shown).
evidence: Stated in the manuscript text.

claim: lin-12 functions cell-autonomously in vm2 to specify vm2 postsynaptic development through regulating muscle arm formation.
source: The mosaic rescue analyses argue that lin-12 functions cell-autonomously in vm2 to specify vm2 postsynaptic development through regulating muscle arm formation.
evidence: Conclusion stated in the manuscript text based on the mosaic rescue analyses.

claim: A lin-12(w750); apx-1(wy755) double mutant did not show an enhanced muscle arm defect.
source: A lin-12(wy750); apx-1(wy755) double mutant did not show an enhanced muscle arm defect (Figure 4D) or more severe egg-laying phenotype (Figure 2A), further suggesting that apx-1 and lin-12 function in the same pathway.
evidence: Stated in the manuscript text with reference to Figure 4D and Figure 2A.

claim: apx-1 and lin-12 function in the same pathway.
source: A lin-12(wy750); apx-1(wy755) double mutant did not show an enhanced muscle arm defect (Figure 4D) or more severe egg-laying phenotype (Figure 2A), further suggesting that apx-1 and lin-12 function in the same pathway.
evidence: Conclusion stated in the manuscript text based on the double mutant phenotype.

claim: The expression of apx-1 was observed in both secondary vulval epithelial cells and vm1 muscle cells during the L4 stage.
source: We observed the expression of apx-1 in both secondary vulval epithelial cells and vm1 muscle cells during the L4 stage, when LIN-12/Notch signaling was activated to promote vm2 muscle arm development (Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Stated in the manuscript text with reference to Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Both secondary vulval epithelial cells and vm1 cells contact vm2 muscle cells from early L4 stage when vulval muscles are generated.
source: Both secondary vulval epithelial cells and vm1 cells contact vm2 muscle cells from early L4 stage when vulval muscles are generated (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C, data not shown, and personal communication with Kelly Liu, July 2012).
evidence: Stated in the manuscript text with reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and personal communication.

claim: The vm2 muscle arms consistently tracked the cell junctions between the primary and secondary vulval epithelial cells.
source: In fact, we observed that the vm2 muscle arms consistently tracked the cell junctions between the primary and secondary vulval epithelial cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and data not shown).

claim: Cell-specific expression of apx-1 in either secondary vulval epithelial cells or vm1 muscle cells rescued the muscle arm defects of apx-1(wy755) mutants.
source: Cell-specific expression of apx-1 in either secondary vulval epithelial cells or vm1 muscle cells rescued the muscle arm defects of apx-1(wy755) mutants (Figure 4F).
evidence: Stated in the manuscript text with reference to Figure 4F.

claim: apx-1 functions in the vm1 and secondary vulval epithelial cells to activate LIN-12/Notch signaling in vm2, the postsynaptic target cells.
source: These data strongly suggest that apx-1 functions in the vm1 and secondary vulval epithelial cells to activate LIN-12/Notch signaling in vm2, the postsynaptic target cells.
evidence: Conclusion stated in the manuscript text based on the cell-specific rescue experiments.

claim: Expression of sel-12 in vulval muscle cells completely rescued the vm2 muscle arm phenotype of sel-12(wy760).
source: We found that expression of sel-12 in vulval muscle cells completely rescued the vm2 muscle arm phenotype of sel-12(wy760), consistent with the cell-autonomous requirement of LIN-12/Notch signaling in vm2 (Figure 4F).
evidence: Stated in the manuscript text with reference to Figure 4F.

claim: Specific expression of a dominant-negative lag-1 construct in the vulval muscles phenocopied the muscle arm defects observed in lin-12(wy750), apx-1(wy750) and sel-12(wy760) mutants.
source: Additionally, specific expression of a dominant-negative lag-1 construct (Kato et al., 1997) in the vulval muscles phenocopied the muscle arm defects observed in lin-12(wy750), apx-1(wy750) and sel-12(wy760) mutants (Figure 4F), suggesting that the canonical LIN-12/Notch pathway is likely involved by controlling the transcription of downstream genes.
evidence: Stated in the manuscript text with reference to Figure 4F and citation to Kato et al., 1997.

claim: The canonical LIN-12/Notch pathway is likely involved by controlling the transcription of downstream genes.
source: Additionally, specific expression of a dominant-negative lag-1 construct (Kato et al., 1997) in the vulval muscles phenocopied the muscle arm defects observed in lin-12(wy750), apx-1(wy750) and sel-12(wy760) mutants (Figure 4F), suggesting that the canonical LIN-12/Notch pathway is likely involved by controlling the transcription of downstream genes.

claim: The expression of a hlh-29 transcription reporter (hlh-29::gfp) was dramatically down-regulated in lin-12(wy750), apx-1(wy755) and sel-12(wy760) mutants.

claim: APX-1 expressed in the secondary vulval epithelial cells and vm1 cells activates the canonical LIN-12/Notch pathway in vm2 to promote the formation of the postsynaptic muscle arms.
source: Together, these results strongly support the model that APX-1 expressed in the secondary vulval epithelial cells and vm1 cells activates the canonical LIN-12/Notch pathway in vm2 to promote the formation of the postsynaptic muscle arms.
evidence: Conclusion stated in the manuscript text based on the experimental results.

claim: The specific activation of the LIN-12/Notch pathway in vm2 but not in vm1 appears to dictate the choice of the synaptic target.
source: The specific activation of the LIN-12/Notch pathway in vm2 but not in vm1 thus appears to dictate the choice of the synaptic target.
evidence: Conclusion stated in the manuscript text based on the experimental results.

claim: apx-1(wy755) mutant animals showed significantly reduced expression of lin-12 in vm2 cells compared with wild-type animals.

claim: The lin-12 expression in vulval epithelial cells was not affected in apx-1(wy755) mutants.
source: Compared with wild-type animals, apx-1(wy755) mutant animals showed significantly reduced expression of lin-12 in vm2 cells, whereas the lin-12 expression in vulval epithelial cells was not affected (Figure 5B,C).
evidence: Stated in the manuscript text with reference to Figure 5B,C.

claim: No change of apx-1 expression was observed in the lin-12(wy750) mutant.

evidence: Stated in the manuscript text with reference to Figure 5D.

claim: apx-1 unilaterally promotes lin-12 expression and activates the LIN-12/Notch pathway in vm2.
source: These results argue that apx-1 unilaterally promotes lin-12 expression and activates the LIN-12/Notch pathway in vm2.

claim: Three LAG-1 consensus binding sites were found in the promoter region of lin-12.

claim: lin-12(e2621) has a 541-bp deletion in the promoter region leading to the deletion of two of the three LAG-1 binding sites.

claim: The muscle arm development was similarly affected in lin-12(e2621).

claim: The muscle arm development might require the positive transcriptional feedback of the LIN-12/Notch pathway.
source: Interestingly, the muscle arm development was similarly affected in lin-12(e2621) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B, bottom), suggesting that the muscle arm development might require the positive transcriptional feedback of the LIN-12/Notch pathway.

claim: UNC-40 is a homolog of Deleted in Colorectal Carcinoma (DCC) and neogenin in vertebrates serving as a receptor for the UNC-6/Netrin ligand.
source: UNC-40, which is a homolog of Deleted in Colorectal Carcinoma (DCC) and neogenin in vertebrates serving as a receptor for the UNC-6/Netrin ligand (Serafini et al., 1994; Chan et al., 1996; Keino-Masu et al., 1996), was reported to play a role in muscle arm formation in the body wall muscles (Dixon and Roy, 2005; Alexander et al., 2009).
evidence: Stated in the manuscript text with citations to multiple prior studies.

claim: UNC-40 was reported to play a role in muscle arm formation in the body wall muscles.
source: UNC-40, which is a homolog of Deleted in Colorectal Carcinoma (DCC) and neogenin in vertebrates serving as a receptor for the UNC-6/Netrin ligand (Serafini et al., 1994; Chan et al., 1996; Keino-Masu et al., 1996), was reported to play a role in muscle arm formation in the body wall muscles (Dixon and Roy, 2005; Alexander et al., 2009).
evidence: Stated in the manuscript text with citations to Dixon and Roy, 2005 and Alexander et al., 2009.

claim: MADD-2 was shown to directly bind and function together with UNC-40 to regulate body wall muscle arm extension as well as axon branching and patterning.
source: More recently, MADD-2, a C1-TRIM protein encoding a homolog of human MID1, was shown to directly bind and function together with UNC-40 to regulate body wall muscle arm extension as well as axon branching and patterning (Alexander et al., 2010; Hao et al., 2010; Morikawa et al., 2011).
evidence: Stated in the manuscript text with citations to Alexander et al., 2010, Hao et al., 2010, and Morikawa et al., 2011.

claim: Both unc-40(n324) and madd-2(ok2226) null mutants showed specific vulval muscle arm defects with largely normal vulval muscle morphology.
source: Interestingly, both unc-40(n324) and madd-2(ok2226) null mutants showed specific vulval muscle arm defects with largely normal vulval muscle morphology (Figure 6A and Figure 1—figure supplement 6).
evidence: Stated in the manuscript text with reference to Figure 6A and Figure 1—figure supplement 6.

claim: A significant proportion of the unc-40 and madd-2 mutant animals completely lacked the vm2 muscle arms.
source: A significant proportion of the mutant animals completely lacked the vm2 muscle arms, while some other animals showed abnormal muscle arms that extended from incorrect positions or flimsy muscle arms that were thinner and dimmer than the wild-type muscle arms (Figure 6B).
evidence: Stated in the manuscript text with reference to Figure 6B.

claim: Some unc-40 and madd-2 mutant animals showed abnormal muscle arms that extended from incorrect positions or flimsy muscle arms that were thinner and dimmer than the wild-type muscle arms.
source: A significant proportion of the mutant animals completely lacked the vm2 muscle arms, while some other animals showed abnormal muscle arms that extended from incorrect positions or flimsy muscle arms that were thinner and dimmer than the wild-type muscle arms (Figure 6B).
evidence: Stated in the manuscript text with reference to Figure 6B.

claim: The muscle arm defects in unc-40 and madd-2 mutants were strongly rescued by expressing unc-40 or madd-2 specifically in vulval muscles in respective mutants.
source: These defects were strongly rescued by expressing unc-40 or madd-2 specifically in vulval muscles in respective mutants, suggesting that both unc-40 and madd-2 function cell-autonomously in vm2 to promote and guide muscle arm growth (Figure 6B).
evidence: Stated in the manuscript text with reference to Figure 6B.

claim: Both unc-40 and madd-2 function cell-autonomously in vm2 to promote and guide muscle arm growth.
source: These defects were strongly rescued by expressing unc-40 or madd-2 specifically in vulval muscles in respective mutants, suggesting that both unc-40 and madd-2 function cell-autonomously in vm2 to promote and guide muscle arm growth (Figure 6B).
evidence: Conclusion stated in the manuscript text based on the cell-specific rescue experiments.

claim: The expression of both unc-40 and madd-2 could be robustly detected in the vm2 cells but not in vm1 cells.
source: Consistent with this notion, we found that the expression of both unc-40 and madd-2 could be robustly detected in the vm2 cells but not in vm1 cells (Figure 6C,D).
evidence: Stated in the manuscript text with reference to Figure 6C,D.

claim: UNC-40::GFP is enriched on the muscle arms.
source: Moreover, UNC-40::GFP is enriched on the muscle arms, further suggesting that it might function locally to promote muscle arm growth (Figure 6C).
evidence: Stated in the manuscript text with reference to Figure 6C.

claim: The levels of UNC-40 and MADD-2 critically determine the capacity of vulval muscles to grow muscle arms and be selected as the postsynaptic target by the egg-laying motoneurons.
source: These results indicate that the levels of UNC-40 and MADD-2 critically determine the capacity of vulval muscles to grow muscle arms and be selected as the postsynaptic target by the egg-laying motoneurons.
evidence: Conclusion stated in the manuscript text based on the experimental results.

claim: The expression of both UNC-40 and MADD-2 in vm2 was significantly down-regulated in the lin-12(wy750) mutant.
source: In wild-type animals, both UNC-40 and MADD-2 translational reporters were preferentially expressed in vm2 cells (Figure 6C,D). UNC-40::GFP showed membrane-associated pattern and was enriched on vm2 muscle arms. MADD-2 was distributed diffusely in vm2 cells. The expression of both UNC-40 and MADD-2 in vm2 was significantly down-regulated in the lin-12(wy750) mutant (Figure 6C,D), supporting the idea that lin-12 was required for the expression of unc-40 and madd-2 in vm2.
evidence: Stated in the manuscript text with reference to Figure 6C,D.

claim: lin-12 is required for the expression of unc-40 and madd-2 in vm2.
source: The expression of both UNC-40 and MADD-2 in vm2 was significantly down-regulated in the lin-12(wy750) mutant (Figure 6C,D), supporting the idea that lin-12 was required for the expression of unc-40 and madd-2 in vm2.
evidence: Conclusion stated in the manuscript text based on the expression analyses.

claim: Both unc-40 and madd-2 are preferentially transcribed in vm2 cells.
source: Similar transcription pattern was observed for unc-40 and madd-2. Both unc-40 and madd-2 were preferentially transcribed in vm2 cells, and the transcriptional activities of both promoters were dramatically suppressed in the lin-12(wy750) mutant (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Stated in the manuscript text with reference to Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: The transcriptional activities of both unc-40 and madd-2 promoters were dramatically suppressed in the lin-12(wy750) mutant.
source: Similar transcription pattern was observed for unc-40 and madd-2. Both unc-40 and madd-2 were preferentially transcribed in vm2 cells, and the transcriptional activities of both promoters were dramatically suppressed in the lin-12(wy750) mutant (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Stated in the manuscript text with reference to Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: The canonical LIN-12/Notch signaling pathway acts to promote the transcriptions of both unc-40 and madd-2 directly.
source: These data indicate that the canonical LIN-12/Notch signaling pathway acts to promote the transcriptions of both unc-40 and madd-2 directly.

claim: Two LAG-1 consensus binding sites were found on the proximal promoter region of the madd-2 gene.
source: Consistent with this model, two LAG-1 consensus binding sites were found on the proximal promoter region of the madd-2 gene.
evidence: Stated in the manuscript text.

claim: Two LAG-1 binding sites were found in the third intron of unc-40 that is essential for its expression.
source: Although no LAG-1 binding site was found in unc-40 promoter region, two were found in the third intron of unc-40 that is essential for its expression (Chan et al., 1996; Christensen et al., 1996; Maier and Gessler, 2000; Personal communication with Daniel Colon-Ramos, January 2013).

claim: unc-40 has a deterministic role in promoting postsynaptic muscle arm development.
source: We found that the expression of unc-40, but not madd-2, in the lin-12(wy750) mutant was sufficient to induced muscle arm-like membrane extension in vm2 cells in ∼41% (36 of 88) of the animal (Figure 7A and data not shown), suggestive of a deterministic role of unc-40 in promoting postsynaptic muscle arm development.
evidence: Conclusion stated in the manuscript text based on the rescue experiment.

claim: Misexpression of UNC-40 was sufficient to induce the dendritic spine-like membrane extensions from vm1 cells.
